label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
To: timeline
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: none

Spent the last two Saturdays redoing a shed for a buddy. I've been doing this for 26 years and I still wasn't ready for what was in there.

When I got the panel door open, my wife was standing behind me. She looked at the inside of the door, where someone had written in Sharpie SHED - DONT TOUCH - RON, and goes, "Who's Ron?" Like I'd know. I don't know Ron. Nobody knows Ron. I think Ron is a myth.

Here's the highlights reel of what we found:

Power to the shed came from three orange extension cords daisy-chained out a basement window, across the yard, and under the deck. Those cords were the best part of the setup, somehow.

One splice was wrapped in duct tape. Not electrical tape. Duct tape. I want to be clear about that because I've gotten a lot of questions.

The shed circuit was on a 30 amp breaker feeding 14 gauge wire. The wire was rated for 15 at best, and the breaker was just sitting there hoping for the best.

The shed outlet was wired with speaker wire. Speaker wire. For a 120 volt outlet. Somebody thought that was fine.

The "GFCI" outlet was a regular outlet with a GFCI sticker stuck on it. That's not a GFCI. That's a sticker with ambition.

The ceiling fan box was held up by one drywall screw. One. It was doing its best.

There was a mouse nest in the junction box. The mice were fine. Honestly, they were the only ones in that shed who seemed to know what they were doing and were unbothered by any of it.

I'm not going to say this guy was evil. He wasn't. He was cheap and a little proud of himself, which is honestly most of what I find in these jobs. He saved a few hundred bucks, felt like a genius, and wrote his name on the door so the next guy would know who to blame. Ron, if you're out there, I hope you're enjoying retirement.

The fix took two Saturdays. We trenched 18 inches down, ran 12/2 UF cable, put in a 20 amp GFCI breaker, a real box, real outlets, and braced the fan properly. Payment was two pizzas and a case of Yuengling. Fair trade, I think.

Here's the part I need people to hear, even if you laugh at all of the above. This stuff starts fires. The shed didn't burn down, but it was about one bad night from doing it. Extension cords under a deck, duct tape on a splice, and a fan hanging from one screw is how houses burn. Most of the time nobody even knows what they're looking at until something smells like it's cooking.

If you're doing electrical work, get a licensed electrician. Pull a permit. Get it inspected. And if your plan is "my buddy watched some videos on YouTube and said he could do it cheap," please don't. The videos don't show you what's behind the drywall. A licensed guy does, and he's the one who'll still be standing there if something goes wrong.

Pics coming below. Judge the duct tape for yourself.
